NEW YORK (CNN) — At CNN’s inaugural Fit Nation Summit, former President Bill Clinton described obesity as the most serious health emergency facing the United States and warned that the country could face grave consequences unless action is taken quickly.

CNN’s chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, joined Clinton in leading the summit’s discussion.

“We need to do something about it for our children, and for our country, because something like this could easily collapse our nation if we don’t act now,” Clinton said.

On Wednesday, Clinton and Gupta brought together specialists from around the country to examine ways to address the nation’s obesity problem.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, two out of every three American adults are overweight or obese, as are one in three children in the United States. Obesity is linked to a greater chance of developing numerous medical conditions, among them high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease and arthritis.

Gupta, Clinton and a group of experts discussed several possible responses, including improving school meals, removing trans fats, expanding access to healthier foods in cities and strengthening local community efforts aimed at reducing obesity.

Clinton, who has worked on the issue in recent years through his Alliance for a Healthier Generation, emphasized that people must be taught the value of eating well and being physically active together.

He acknowledged that encouraging Americans — particularly children — to change their habits will be difficult.

“They need to be handled with care. Kids need to know it’s important, but [fitness] can’t be boring,” Clinton said. “There’s no shame, there’s no embarrassment. We have to let them know it’s all good, but you have to do it.”

Michael Jacobson, executive director of the Center for Science in the Public Interest and a prominent opponent of trans fats in food, said the Food and Drug Administration should prohibit trans fats nationwide rather than leaving decisions to state and local authorities.

Trans fats were once considered useful replacements for other fats, but research over time has shown that they increase LDL, or “bad,” cholesterol while reducing HDL, or “good,” cholesterol.

“They’re just not good for our health,” Jacobson said.

Dr. Robert Eckel, a former president of the American Heart Association, voiced a note of caution: “Although we support the removal of trans fats, our biggest concern is what they’ll be replaced with. We need to think about that, because there will be a substitute.”

The panel also answered questions from an audience of 150 people, most of whom were obesity specialists or professionals working in fields connected to the issue.

Gupta was motivated to create Fit Nation as a continuing, multiplatform, grass-roots campaign against obesity. During the previous three years, Gupta and the CNN Medical Unit traveled around the United States, urging people to manage their weight by becoming more active and eating better.

This year, Gupta went from Michigan to California, asking Americans to promise to collectively add 1 million hours to their lives by getting off the couch and exercising. Since the tour began in April, the effort has exceeded its target, with pledged exercise time nearing four times the original goal.

Gupta said he wants the ideas discussed at the summit to reach lawmakers and administrators who have the power to shape policy and possibly influence public views about obesity.

“I’ve covered a lot of stories on obesity,” Gupta said. “There’s a battle going on, and we need to win the battle. I’ve talked to people out there and many are just blasé.

“This is our opportunity to make them care.”

Former President Bill Clinton, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, and a group of leading health experts used CNN’s Fit Nation Summit to draw attention to what they described as one of the most urgent public health challenges facing the United States: obesity. The discussion focused on the scale of the problem, its causes, and the kinds of national and community-based solutions that could help reverse current trends.

Participants noted that obesity is no longer a concern affecting only a small portion of the population. With roughly two-thirds of American adults and about one-third of children now considered overweight or obese, the issue has become a widespread health crisis. Experts warned that these numbers are tied to rising rates of diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, certain cancers, and other serious medical conditions. They also stressed that childhood obesity is especially alarming because unhealthy habits and health problems that begin early in life can continue into adulthood.

Former President Clinton emphasized that the country must treat obesity as a shared national responsibility rather than simply an individual problem. He and other speakers argued that many Americans live in environments that make unhealthy choices easier and healthier choices harder. In some neighborhoods, especially low-income communities, fresh fruits, vegetables, and affordable nutritious foods are difficult to find. At the same time, fast food, processed snacks, and sugary drinks are often cheap, convenient, and heavily marketed.

The summit explored several possible solutions. Improving school lunches was highlighted as a major priority, since children consume many of their daily calories at school. Health experts said schools can play an important role by serving more nutritious meals, limiting access to unhealthy snacks and sugary beverages, and teaching students about food, exercise, and long-term health. They also discussed the importance of physical education and giving children more opportunities to be active during the school day.

Another topic was the role of government policy. Speakers pointed to measures such as banning trans fats, improving food labeling, and encouraging healthier standards in restaurants and public institutions. They argued that policy changes can help shift the food environment in ways that benefit everyone, not just those with the time and resources to seek out healthier options on their own.

Urban planning and access to healthy food were also part of the conversation. Experts said communities need grocery stores, farmers markets, safe parks, sidewalks, and recreation spaces so that people can eat better and exercise more easily. In areas sometimes described as “food deserts,” residents may have limited access to fresh, affordable food, making it harder to maintain a healthy diet. Addressing these gaps, participants said, is essential to reducing health disparities.

Education was another major theme. Dr. Gupta and others stressed that people need clear, practical information about nutrition, portion sizes, physical activity, and the risks of obesity-related disease. However, they also noted that education alone is not enough. People must have realistic opportunities to act on what they learn, which means healthier food must be accessible and affordable, and physical activity must be built into daily life.

Community-based programs were presented as an important part of the solution. Local initiatives involving schools, parents, doctors, businesses, faith groups, and civic organizations can help create healthier habits where people live and work. These programs may include walking groups, after-school sports, cooking classes, nutrition counseling, workplace wellness efforts, and campaigns to reduce sugary drink consumption.

Throughout the summit, the speakers warned that failure to act could have serious consequences beyond individual health. Rising obesity rates could place enormous pressure on the health care system, increase medical costs, reduce workplace productivity, and affect military readiness and overall quality of life. The social and economic effects, they argued, make obesity not only a medical issue but also a national concern.

The central message of the Fit Nation Summit was that obesity is preventable, but prevention requires coordinated action. Families, schools, communities, health professionals, businesses, and government leaders all have roles to play. By improving nutrition, increasing physical activity, creating healthier environments, and supporting long-term behavior change, the experts said the United States can begin to reverse the obesity epidemic and protect future generations from its most damaging consequences.

**Bill Clinton urges national action on obesity at CNN Fit Nation Summit**

Former President Bill Clinton called America’s obesity crisis “one of the defining public health challenges of our time” during remarks at CNN’s first Fit Nation Summit, joining medical experts, educators and community leaders in a discussion focused on improving nutrition, increasing physical activity and reshaping the environments where Americans live, work and learn.

The summit, moderated in part by CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta, brought attention to rising rates of obesity among adults and children and the long-term health consequences tied to poor diet and sedentary lifestyles.

“We have to make the healthy choice the easy choice,” Clinton said, emphasizing that lasting change will require cooperation among families, schools, businesses, health care providers and local governments.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, obesity affects more than 40% of U.S. adults and nearly 20% of children and adolescents. The CDC links obesity to increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, stroke, certain cancers and higher health care costs.

Gupta noted that the numbers represent more than statistics. “This is about what happens in a doctor’s office, in a school cafeteria, in a grocery store and on a neighborhood street,” he said. “Health is shaped long before someone becomes a patient.”

A major focus of the summit was childhood nutrition, including the role of school lunches. Clinton, whose foundation has worked on childhood health initiatives, said schools can be a powerful starting point by offering healthier meals, reducing sugary drinks and creating more opportunities for physical activity.

Panelists discussed how reforming school food programs can help children develop healthier habits early in life. They pointed to efforts in some districts to increase fresh fruits and vegetables, use whole grains and reduce highly processed foods.

The conversation also turned to trans fats, once common in fried and packaged foods. Public health advocates credited restrictions on artificial trans fats as an example of how policy can improve health outcomes on a broad scale. The FDA has determined that partially hydrogenated oils, the primary dietary source of artificial trans fats, are not generally recognized as safe, leading manufacturers to remove them from many products.

Speakers said similar approaches could be used to improve access to nutritious foods, limit unhealthy marketing to children and encourage food manufacturers to reduce excess sugar and sodium.

Community-level solutions were another central theme. Participants highlighted programs that bring farmers markets to underserved neighborhoods, create safe walking and biking routes, expand parks and recreation spaces, and partner with local clinics to screen residents for obesity-related conditions.

Clinton said the country must avoid framing obesity as simply a matter of individual willpower. “People make choices within the choices they have,” he said. “If a community has no grocery store, no safe place to walk and a school lunch program under pressure, then we have to change those conditions.”

Gupta echoed that point, saying successful obesity prevention depends on combining personal responsibility with public support. “Exercise matters. Food choices matter. But access matters too,” he said.

The summit ended with a call for coordinated action, from healthier school meals and workplace wellness efforts to better urban planning and expanded preventive care.

“We know enough to act,” Clinton said. “The question is whether we have the will to build communities that help people live healthier lives.”

# Obesity increasingly seen as America’s leading health crisis

**By Staff Writer**

Obesity has emerged as one of the most urgent public health challenges in the United States, touching nearly every corner of American life — from hospitals and schools to workplaces, grocery aisles and family dinner tables.

Public health experts say the condition is no longer just a matter of individual behavior. It is a nationwide crisis shaped by food policy, poverty, marketing, sedentary lifestyles, medical access and the built environment.

More than 40% of American adults have obesity, according to federal health data, and the condition is linked to some of the country’s most serious and costly diseases, including Type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, certain cancers and kidney disease.

Former President Bill Clinton, whose own health history led him to become more publicly engaged on diet and wellness, has often spoken about the importance of prevention and healthier eating. **[Insert verified Clinton quote here.]**

Medical experts say the scale of the problem is difficult to overstate.

Dr. Sanjay Gupta, CNN’s chief medical correspondent and a practicing neurosurgeon, has reported extensively on the connections between diet, exercise, chronic illness and public health. **[Insert verified Gupta quote here.]**

## A crisis years in the making

The rise in obesity did not happen overnight. Over several decades, Americans have consumed more ultra-processed foods, larger portions and sugary beverages, while many communities have become less walkable and more dependent on cars.

Michael Jacobson, longtime nutrition advocate and co-founder of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, has been a prominent critic of food industry marketing and the prevalence of calorie-dense, nutrient-poor products. **[Insert verified Jacobson quote here.]**

Nutrition researchers say the American food environment often makes the unhealthy choice the easiest and cheapest one. Fast food is widely available, processed snacks are heavily advertised, and many families lack reliable access to affordable fresh produce.

At the same time, obesity remains highly stigmatized — a factor doctors say can keep patients from seeking care.

## Medical risks and economic costs

Dr. Robert Eckel, a cardiologist and former president of the American Heart Association, has emphasized the connection between excess weight and cardiovascular disease. **[Insert verified Eckel quote here.]**

The medical consequences are vast. Obesity increases the risk of high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, insulin resistance and inflammation — all factors that can contribute to heart disease.

The economic burden is also significant. Obesity-related health care costs run into the hundreds of billions of dollars annually, according to several estimates. Employers, insurers, government programs and families all absorb the cost through medical bills, lost productivity and disability.

## New treatments, old questions

Recent advances in weight-loss medications, including GLP-1 drugs, have transformed the conversation around obesity treatment. Many physicians now describe obesity as a chronic disease that often requires long-term medical management, not simply willpower.

But the medications are expensive, not always covered by insurance, and may need to be taken indefinitely to maintain weight loss. That has raised questions about access and equity.

Public health experts say medical treatment alone cannot solve the crisis. They argue that prevention must include healthier school meals, clearer food labeling, limits on junk-food marketing to children, safer spaces for physical activity and policies that make nutritious food more affordable.

## Beyond personal responsibility

For decades, obesity was framed largely as a personal failure. That view is changing.

Doctors and public health leaders increasingly describe obesity as the result of biology interacting with an environment that promotes weight gain. Genetics, stress, sleep, medications, income, neighborhood design and food access can all play a role.

The challenge, experts say, is to address obesity without blaming people who live with it.

America’s obesity crisis is not just about weight. It is about the nation’s food system, health care system, economy and culture — and whether the country can shift from treating disease after it develops to preventing it before it starts.

A panel of public health experts, physicians, educators and community advocates called for a “whole-environment” approach to reducing obesity, arguing that individual willpower alone cannot solve a crisis shaped by school meals, food marketing, neighborhood design, workplace habits and access to affordable healthy foods.

The discussion focused on practical strategies already gaining traction in schools, cities and media campaigns: improving school lunches, eliminating industrial trans fats, expanding physical activity programs and using public education initiatives—such as CNN’s **Fit Nation**, led by chief medical correspondent **Dr. Sanjay Gupta**—to help Americans adopt healthier routines.

Panelists emphasized that obesity is linked to increased risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, sleep apnea, some cancers and joint problems. But they also warned against framing obesity as a personal failure, noting that genetics, income, stress, food access, medications, sleep and community conditions all influence weight.

“People make choices, but choices are shaped by the world around them,” one public health speaker said. “If the default options are cheap ultra-processed food, unsafe streets and no time for exercise, we shouldn’t be surprised when obesity rates rise.”

## Healthier school lunches seen as a starting point

Much of the conversation centered on children, with panelists arguing that schools are one of the most important places to build lifelong habits.

Experts recommended meals with more fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins and lower-fat dairy, while reducing added sugars, sodium and highly processed foods. Several panelists also stressed the importance of making healthier food appealing to students rather than simply placing it on the tray.

Suggestions included salad bars, culturally familiar recipes, scratch cooking, taste tests, farm-to-school programs and involving students in menu decisions.

“Healthy school lunches cannot feel like punishment,” an education advocate said. “If students throw the food away, we have not solved the problem. Nutrition has to meet taste, culture and convenience.”

Panelists also noted that school meals are especially important for children from low-income families, who may rely on breakfast and lunch programs for a large share of their daily nutrition. Improving those meals, they said, can reduce health disparities while supporting learning, concentration and attendance.

## Trans fat bans cited as a public health success

The panel also pointed to the removal of artificial trans fats from the food supply as an example of policy that can improve health without requiring consumers to become nutrition experts.

Artificial trans fats, often found in partially hydrogenated oils, were once common in baked goods, fried foods and packaged snacks. They raise LDL, or “bad,” cholesterol and lower HDL, or “good,” cholesterol, increasing the risk of heart disease.

Public health officials have credited trans fat restrictions and bans with helping reduce cardiovascular risk at the population level. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration determined that partially hydrogenated oils were no longer “generally recognized as safe,” leading to their removal from most foods.

Panelists said the lesson is that some health interventions work best when they change the environment rather than relying on consumers to read every label.

“No one misses trans fats,” a physician on the panel said. “That’s the point. When the food supply gets healthier, millions of people benefit quietly.”

## Exercise campaigns must be realistic, panelists say

Physical activity was another major focus, but experts cautioned against promoting exercise only through intense gym culture or weight-loss messaging.

Instead, they called for campaigns that encourage walking, biking, dancing, sports, active commuting, stair use and short movement breaks during the day. The panel highlighted the federal guideline that adults aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, along with muscle-strengthening activities at least two days weekly. Children and teens are generally encouraged to get about 60 minutes of physical activity daily.

But panelists said communities must make movement easier and safer. That includes sidewalks, parks, bike lanes, recreation centers, school sports, after-school programs and safe routes to school.

“Exercise advice only goes so far if a neighborhood has no sidewalks or parents don’t feel safe letting children play outside,” one community health leader said.

The panel also noted that physical activity improves blood pressure, insulin sensitivity, mood, sleep and cardiovascular fitness—even when the number on the scale does not change dramatically.

## CNN’s Fit Nation highlighted as media-driven motivation

The discussion also referenced CNN’s **Fit Nation** initiative, associated with Dr. Sanjay Gupta, as an example of how media can encourage healthier lifestyles by making fitness goals visible and relatable.

Fit Nation has featured ordinary people working toward major health and fitness milestones, including endurance events, while receiving coaching and medical guidance. Panelists said programs like it can help demystify exercise, especially when they show gradual progress, setbacks and sustainable behavior change rather than instant transformation.

Dr. Gupta, a neurosurgeon and longtime medical journalist, has used the platform to connect personal health stories with broader public health messages. Panelists said that kind of storytelling can be powerful because many people respond more strongly to real-life examples than to statistics alone.

However, several experts cautioned that fitness campaigns should avoid implying that everyone needs to become an athlete. For many people, they said, the first step may be a 10-minute walk, cooking one more meal at home each week or replacing sugary drinks with water.

“The best program is the one people can actually maintain,” a panelist said. “Inspiration matters, but sustainability matters more.”

## Obesity solutions require policy and compassion

Panelists repeatedly returned to the idea that obesity prevention and treatment require multiple tools at once. Among the strategies discussed:

- Stronger nutrition standards for school meals  
- Limits on artificial trans fats and other harmful food additives  
- Clearer food labeling  
- More access to affordable fruits, vegetables and minimally processed foods  
- Physical education and daily movement opportunities in schools  
- Safe public spaces for walking and recreation  
- Workplace wellness efforts that encourage movement without stigma  
- Medical care that includes nutrition counseling, behavioral support and, when appropriate, anti-obesity medications or bariatric surgery  
- Public messaging that promotes health without shaming people  

The panel also addressed weight stigma, warning that shame can discourage people from seeking care and may worsen mental and physical health. Clinicians, educators and policymakers, they said, should focus on health behaviors, metabolic risk and supportive environments rather than blame.

## A long-term public health challenge

The panel concluded that obesity is not likely to be reversed by any single program, diet or campaign. Instead, participants urged coordinated action across government, schools, health care, media, food companies and local communities.

Healthy school lunches can shape habits early. Trans fat bans can remove hidden risks from the food supply. Exercise campaigns can make movement more normal and accessible. Media initiatives like Fit Nation can motivate people by showing that change is possible.

But the overarching message was that lasting progress depends on making healthier choices easier, more affordable and more realistic.

“Obesity is a medical issue, a social issue and an environmental issue,” one panelist said. “If we want healthier people, we have to build healthier places to live, learn, work and eat.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN news piece beginning “NEW YORK (CNN) -- Obesity is the No. 1 health crisis in the United States,” describing Clinton and Gupta’s Fit Nation Summit and the campaign to get Americans exercising.
counterfactuals.output:
NEW YORK (CNN) -- Obesity is the No. 1 health crisis in the United States, and former President Bill Clinton joined CNN’s Dr. Sanjay Gupta at a Fit Nation Summit to urge Americans to move more, eat better and rethink the way the country approaches health.

The event brought together doctors, fitness experts, educators, business leaders and community advocates to discuss practical ways to fight obesity, diabetes and heart disease — conditions closely linked to sedentary lifestyles and poor nutrition.

Clinton, who has spoken publicly about his own heart health and lifestyle changes, said the nation must make wellness easier for families, children and workers.

“We have to create conditions where the healthy choice is the easy choice,” Clinton said, emphasizing access to safe places to exercise, healthier school meals and workplace wellness programs.

Gupta, CNN’s chief medical correspondent, focused on the simple message behind the Fit Nation campaign: Americans do not have to become elite athletes to improve their health. Regular walking, small dietary changes and consistent daily movement can lower risks for chronic disease.

Public health experts at the summit said the challenge is not just personal willpower. Many communities lack sidewalks, parks, affordable fresh food and time for physical activity. The speakers called for partnerships among schools, employers, local governments and health care providers to help people build exercise into everyday life.

The campaign encourages Americans to set realistic goals — taking the stairs, walking 30 minutes a day, reducing sugary drinks and involving families in active routines. Organizers said even modest changes, sustained over time, can make a measurable difference.

For Clinton and Gupta, the message was urgent but optimistic: reversing the obesity epidemic will require national commitment, but it starts with individual steps — literally.

“Fitness isn’t about perfection,” Gupta said. “It’s about momentum. If we can get people moving, we can change the health of the country.”
